lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Owned the claims backlog report and the weekly numbers the claims managers used.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved reporting efficiency by 90% by moving the monthly revenue report to scheduled SQL queries.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.
- Wrote data-quality checks on the 40 most-used tables, catching 15 broken loads before they reached a dashboard.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Reported the national conversion rate as the simple average of 14 regional conversion rates, without weighting by regional traffic.
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Compared the forecast with the operator's rebalancing schedule: empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week in a replay of last summer.
- Published the notebooks and a short write-up, which the city's open-data team linked from its bike-share page.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Built a retention dashboard for about 2.4 million shoppers that raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The résumé includes date of birth and nationality, personal details conventionally left off.
items.because: They are not meant to weigh in assessing qualifications and use space without supporting the analyst application.

items.says: The experience entries are not in newest-first order.
items.because: Pinecrest appears above the more recent Brightcart role, making the timeline harder to establish.

items.says: Education appears before several years of relevant analyst experience.
items.because: A reader should encounter the professional background most relevant to an analyst role first.

items.says: The bullet does not say what the weekly figures measured or what claims decision they supported.
“Owned” describes responsibility rather than an action.
The bullet does not say how the claims backlog report was built or checked.
The hold-time reduction is buried after the analysis, and the bullet should appear before the claims-backlog bullet.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the analysis before the clearest evidence of its impact.

items.says: “My findings” uses a first-person pronoun.
items.because: It breaks the résumé’s otherwise impersonal bullet style.

items.says: The analysis does not say what pattern identified the evening peak.
The query-error reduction has no stated baseline or comparison period.
Unrelated support duties crowd the automation result.
items.because: The calendar, sales questions, onboarding documents and help-desk coverage read partly like a task list and distract from the fraud-team result.

items.says: The 10-hour monthly saving has no stated basis.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what prior effort the saving is compared with.

items.says: The bullet does not say what manual step the automation replaced or how the extract ran.
The 90% improvement has no defined efficiency measure.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether it reduced report-preparation time, manual work or another cost, making the figure hard to interpret.

items.says: The null check is on the wrong table: customers with no orders have nulls in orders columns, not customer columns.
items.because: An unmatched customer in a left join from customers to orders still has a non-null customer name.

items.says: The customer finding does not say what it changed or why it mattered.
The bullet does not say what the data-quality checks tested.
The funding result comes after the presentation detail.
items.because: The outcome is easy to miss when scanning.

items.says: The simple average of 14 regional conversion rates is not the national conversion rate.
items.because: A national rate divides total conversions by total traffic, while a simple average gives each region equal weight.

items.says: The bullet does not say what decision or outcome the reported rate informed.
The repeat-purchase result is buried after the dashboard context, and this strongest bullet should appear earlier in the entry.
items.because: A scanning reader may reach the end before seeing its clearest result.

items.says: The forecast error is missing its evaluation basis.
The bullet does not name the modeling approach.
The strongest result in the project is not foregrounded, and its bullet should come first.
items.because: The reduction in empty-station hours would land harder if its bullet came before the modeling bullet.

items.says: “In a replay of last summer” leaves the simulation qualifier until the end.
items.because: A reader reaches the end before learning that the comparison was simulated.

items.says: The bullet does not explain how the forecast was used in the replay.
The city’s link is buried in a relative clause instead of being foregrounded as the outcome.
The Saturday line-cut result comes after the method.
items.because: The outcome is easy to miss.

items.says: The bullet does not state the unique-household count.
items.because: The count is presented as the new measure produced, but the reader cannot see what it revealed.

items.says: The bullet does not say how repeat visitors were matched.
items.because: The matching basis is central to understanding how the count was derived.

items.says: The shopper-retention claim duplicates the Brightcart achievement and does not belong in the pantry project.
items.because: Millions of shoppers and repeat purchases do not fit the pantry context, and the conflicting attribution can make the résumé seem inconsistent.

items.says: The repeat-purchase claim does not state its comparison or timeframe.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what “nearly a quarter” is compared with or over what period.

items.says: The retention-dashboard claim does not say what analytical feature or approach supported the result.
items.because: A reader cannot distinguish the contribution from a generic dashboard task.
